newsitem.title: PERU: Peru looks to relaunch talks with hostage takers.
newsitem.headline: Peru looks to relaunch talks with hostage takers.

text.p: Peru sought on Wednesday to relaunch talks with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for 50 days.
President Alberto Fujimori, returning to Peru after a five-day foreign tour, said on Tuesday his government would do everything it could to free the captives.

"The task which faces us now is to try to look at every imaginative way possible so that the hostages being unjustly held can be liberated," Fujimori told reporters on landing at Lima's international airport.

The Peruvian leader, whose younger brother Pedro is among the captives, promised Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto at a weekend crisis summit in Toronto that he would resume negotiations with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas inside the residence.
There have been no direct talks between the two sides since Dec. 28.
But Fujimori stressed on Tuesday he would stick to his line of "prudence and firmness" in dealing with the rebels.

The MRTA is demanding the release of about 400 jailed comrades in return for a glittering array of hostages which includes two government ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and nearly two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.

Fujimori, who has built a reputation for being tough on Peru's guerrilla movements, rejects this demand but has floated the possibility of easing harsh prison conditions and allowing the hostage takers to seek asylum abroad.

During a brief visit to Washington, where he received strong support from President Bill Clinton for his crisis management on Monday, Fujimori indicated that advances had been made in behind-the-scenes talks with the rebels.
But the two sides continued to trade verbal blows in public on Tuesday.
Just before dawn, MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini commemorated the start of his revolutionary struggle with gunfire and slogans.

After each of the six shots, fired from a lower window of the residence, Cerpa shouted the name of a worker killed when police stormed the Cromotex textile factory near Lima to end a prolonged strike exactly 18 years ago.
"Comrades, take our blood and transform it into the torrent of revolutionary force," Cerpa shouted through a megaphone.

The Cromotex dispute spurred Cerpa to help organise the MRTA and the rebel leader named the Dec. 17 operation to storm the diplomatic mansion after Hemegidio Huertas, one of the workers killed during the strike.
Fujimori slammed the defiant display as evidence of the MRTA's bloody past.
"They are showing themselves for what they are. Today they tried to celebrate an act of blood," he said.
Government officials have said they have selected a building near the residence to hold the talks between Cerpa and government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo.

A team of four "guarantors" -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Japanese crisis point man Terusuke Tarada -- has been nominated to observe any talks.
A bullet-proof vehicle has also been arranged to take Cerpa to the negotiating table.
